label: Digital history
date_label: Earlier roots · selected publications 2003–2022; field chronology unresolved
description: Historical inquiry using digital media to assemble and interpret evidence, develop arguments, publish scholarship, teach and involve public audiences. This selection spans digital projects, computational exploration, preservation and source criticism, including debates over participation, race, gender and scholarly credit. Digital history overlaps with quantitative history, public history and digital humanities without being equivalent to any of them.
scope_note: Bounded selection of projects, methods, public practice and critical reflection. No founding year, complete genealogy or comprehensive field review through 2026 is asserted.

representative_people.context: Cohen and Rosenzweig connect digital history with searchable and recombinable evidence, public participation and collaborative historical communication, while examining problems of authenticity and authority. Selected introduction only. Their account identifies possibilities and hazards, not proof that digital access automatically democratizes history; historical platform examples are not current measurements. Rosenzweig treats digital abundance and the danger of record loss as simultaneous problems for historical research. Opening programme in an authorized transcription; not evidence of a complete digital historical record or of current preservation conditions. representative_people.context: Thomas and Ayers frame a close comparison of two American communities around the relationship between slavery and emergent modernity, asking why profound social differences can coexist with similar measurable indices. Repository author abstract only. Their stated focus is slavery’s relation to white society, not a comprehensive account of enslaved people’s lives; no replication of the comparison or full electronic-article reading is claimed. Thomas argues that digital historical scholarship can connect interpretation, narrative, evidence and spatial analysis, making paths of historical reasoning available to readers. Selected concluding discussion, not endorsement of every earlier genealogy in the chapter. He describes an experimental programme and project design, not an inevitable transformation of the profession. Thomas describes his joint project with Ayers as a prismatic arrangement linking analysis, evidence and historiography, with its digital form intended to carry an argument about slavery’s varied social effects. A participant’s 2004 account of a joint project; not independent validation or a newly originated 2004 project. The electronic article’s full body and technical implementation were not recovered.
representative_people.works: The Differences Slavery Made: A Close Analysis of Two American Communities; Computing and the Historical Imagination

label: Web history / Archived-web research
date_label: Earlier roots · selected publications 2003–2026; field chronology unresolved
description: Historical inquiry into the web and inquiry using archived web evidence. These overlap but differ: web archives also inform political, social and cultural histories whose object is not the web itself. Archival and information scholars contribute contextual methods without being assigned an exclusive historian profession.
scope_note: Bounded selection of projects, methods, public practice and critical reflection. No founding year, complete genealogy or comprehensive field review through 2026 is asserted.
